overview.body:
**Hwanung** ​(*hwanung*) — ‌Son of ‌Heaven, Descended ​· Heavenly ​prince — ​belongs to ​the Korean ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Son of ​Heaven, Descended". ‌The name ​means "Heavenly ‌prince"[^1].

**Hwanung** ​is the ​heavenly prince ​who descends ​from the ​court of ‌Hwanin to ​bring law, ‌agriculture, and ​the arts ‌of civilisation ​to earth ‌in Korean ​tradition. The ‌name means ​"Heavenly prince" ​and belongs ‌to the ‌domain "Son ‌of Heaven, ​Descended." Hwanung ​is the ‌son of ​Hwanin and ​the father ‌of Dangun ​in the ​founding myth ‌cycle recorded ​in the ‌Samguk Yusa. ​He descends ​to earth ​beneath a ​sandalwood tree ‌on a ‌high mountain, ​bringing three ‌heavenly seals ​and three ​thousand retainers.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ‌the name ‌as **Hwanung** ‌and serves ​its temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/hwanung/). The ​restoration needs ​no distinctive ‌letters or ​diacritics its ​ASCII form ​would lose, ‌which places ​the name ​in Tier ​2. The ‌plain ASCII ​form *hwanung* ‌survives as ​a modern ‌convenience imposed ​by the ‌early domain-name ‌system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).
Lee, Peter H., ed., Sourcebook of Korean Civilization, vol. 1 (Columbia University Press, 1993).
Grayson, James H., Korea: A Religious and Cultural History (Routledge, 2002).

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Hangul + ​Hanja ​as **환웅 ​(桓雄)**. ​Etymologically ‌it means ​"Heavenly ​prince"[^1].

The ‌ASCII ​form *hwanung* ‌survives ​only ‌because the ​early ​domain-name system ​could ​not ​carry diacritics; ‌it ​is a ‌technological ​compromise, ‌not an ​ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode ‌restoration ​**Hwanung** recovers ​the ‌full diacritic ‌detail ‌of the ​scholarly ​transliteration ‌directly in ​the ​address bar. ‌The ​restoration ​needs no ‌distinctive ​letters or ‌diacritics ​its ​ASCII form ​would ​lose, which ‌places ‌the ​name in ‌Tier ​2.

The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

‌- ‌**h** ‌→ **H** ​— ‌Same, capitalized
​- ​**w** ​→ **w** ‌— ​Same
- ​**a** ​→ ‌**a** — ​Same
​- **n** ​→ ‌**n** ​— Same
‌- ​**u** → ‌**u** ​— Same
‌- ‌**n** ​→ **n** ​— ​Same
- ​**g** ‌→ ‌**g** — ​Same

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name ​is **/hwa.nuŋ/** ​— ​Korean Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

‌- **hwa** ​— The ​first ‌syllable of ​Hwanung, ‌carrying primary ​stress in ‌the ​romanised form.
​- **nuŋ** ​— ​The middle ​syllable ‌or element, ​pronounced with ‌level ​pitch in ‌Korean.
- ​**-** ‌— The ​final ‌syllable, often ​closing in ​a ‌nasal or ‌simple vowel ‌in ​the Korean ​reading.

‌For the ​modern speaker, ​the ‌closest approximation ​is: 'HWAH-noong' ​— ‌The second ​syllable ‌ends in ​a velar ​nasal, ​like the ​‘ng’ in ‌‘song’. ‌The capitalised ​form ‌marks the ​heavenly prince ​as ‌a proper ‌noun.

Kindred ‌and ‌historical forms ​of ‌the name:

​- **Hangul** ​— ​환웅 — ‌the Korean ​script ​form.
- ​**Hanja** ‌— 桓雄 ​— the ​Sino-Korean ​character form.

‌The second ​syllable ‌ends in ​a ‌velar nasal, ​like the ‌‘ng’ ‌in ‘song’. ​The capitalised ​form ​marks the ​heavenly ‌prince as ‌a proper ​noun.

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved ‌in ​Hangul + ​Hanja ​as **환웅 ​(桓雄)** ​— ‌Korean alphabet ​+ ​Chinese characters, ‌attested ​Modern ‌Korean (Samguk ​Yusa, ‌13th c.), ​in ​Korea. ​The script ​is ​written left-to-right.[^1]

‌The ​scholarly ‌transliteration is ​*Hwanung* ‌(Revised Romanization), ​giving ‌the ​normalized reading ‌/hwan.uŋ/.

​The rendering ​proceeds ‌step ‌by step:

‌- ​Hangul 환웅 ​with ‌Hanja ​桓雄 — ​the ‌heavenly prince ​of ​the ‌Dangun cycle

​Korean ‌names ​may be ​written ​in Hangul, ​the ‌indigenous ‌Korean alphabet, ​and ‌sometimes in ​Hanja, ​the ‌Sino-Korean character ‌set. ‌For **Hwanung**, ‌the ​Hangul ‌form is ​**환웅** ​and the ​Hanja ‌form ​is **桓雄**. ​Hangul ​‘환웅’ and ‌Hanja ​‘桓雄’, ​the forms ​preserved ‌in the ​Samguk ‌Yusa. ​The ASCII ‌form ​*hwanung* is ‌a ‌technological ​compromise; the ​capitalised ​restoration **Hwanung** ​is ‌the ‌scholarly citation ​form.

domains.body:
**Hwanung** ​is the ‌heavenly prince ‌who descends ​from the ​court ​of Hwanin ​to bring ​law, agriculture, ‌and the ​arts ​of civilisation ‌to earth ​in Korean ‌tradition. The ​name means ‌"Heavenly ​prince" and ​belongs to ​the domain ​"Son of ​Heaven, ‌Descended." Hwanung ​is the ‌son of ​Hwanin and ‌the ​father of ‌Dangun in ​the founding ‌myth cycle ​recorded ​in the ‌Samguk Yusa. ‌He descends ‌to earth ​beneath ​a sandalwood ‌tree on ​a high ​mountain, bringing ‌three ​heavenly seals ​and three ‌thousand retainers.[^1]

​### Son ‌of Hwanin

​Hwanung ​carries the ​authority of ​heaven as ‌the delegate ‌of ​his father, ‌the Lord ​of Heaven.

​### Descended ‌to ‌Taebaek

He ‌descends beneath ‌a sandalwood ​tree on ‌a ​high mountain, ​the sacred ​entry point ‌between heaven ​and ​earth.

### ​Law and ‌Agriculture

He ​teaches the ​people ​law, grain, ‌medicine, and ​the crafts ‌that define ​civilised life.

‌### ​Father of ‌Dangun

His ‌union with ​Ungnyeo produces ​Dangun, ​the first ​ancestor and ‌king of ‌the Korean ​people.

sources.citation: Lee, Peter H., ed., Sourcebook of Korean Civilization, vol. 1 (Columbia University Press, 1993).
Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).

mythology.body:
The mythology ​of Hwanung ‌is preserved ‌in Korean ​oral tradition, ​shamanic ritual ​texts, and ​classical sources ​such as ‌the Samguk ​Yusa. The ​narratives are ‌not merely ​stories; they ‌encode social ​values, ritual ‌obligations, and ​relationships between ​humans, nature, ​and the ​sacred. Some ​details vary ‌by region ​and by ‌shamanic lineage.[^1]

​### The ‌Descent from ​Heaven (Samguk ‌Yusa)

Yearning ​to rule the ‌world below, ​Hwanung asked ​his father ‌Hwanin to ‌send him ‌to earth. ​Hwanin granted ​him three ‌heavenly seals ​and three ​thousand retainers, ‌and Hwanung ​descended to ​a sandalwood ‌tree on ​the slopes ‌of a ​high mountain.[^2]

​### The ​Rule of ​Wind and ‌Rain (Foundation ‌myth)

Hwanung ​governed the ‌natural forces ​that sustain ​agriculture: wind, ‌rain, clouds, ‌and grain. ‌Under his rule ‌the people ​learned the ‌arts of ​civilisation, including ​law, medicine, ​and the ‌weaving of ​cloth.

### ​The Birth ​of Dangun ‌(Foundation myth)

​When a ​bear and ​a tiger ‌begged to ​become human, ‌Hwanung tested ​them with ‌garlic and ​mugwort. The ‌bear endured ‌and became ​a woman, ​Ungnyeo; she ​married Hwanung ​and gave ‌birth to ‌Dangun, founder ​of Gojoseon.

sources.citation: Lee, Peter H., ed., Sourcebook of Korean Civilization, vol. 1 (Columbia University Press, 1993).
Grayson, James H., Korea: A Religious and Cultural History (Routledge, 2002).

syncretism.body:
Hwanung ​functions ‌as ‌a ​culture-hero ​in ​the Korean ​mythic ​system, ‌comparable ​to ​other ‌East ​Asian ‌figures ​who ‌descend ​from ​heaven ​to teach ​agriculture ​and ‌law. ​The ‌story ​has ‌been ​read ‌through ​Confucian, ‌Buddhist, ​and Daoist ​lenses, ‌each ‌tradition ‌finding ​in ​it ‌a ​model ​of ‌virtuous ​rule ​or ‌cosmic harmony. ​In ‌modern ​Korean ​nationalism, ​Hwanung ​represents ‌the ‌heavenly ​origin ‌of ​Korean ​civilisation, ‌while in ‌shamanic ‌ritual ‌he ​is ‌remembered ​as ​one ​of ‌the ​high ​spirits ​of the ‌celestial ​pantheon.[^1]

​Within ​the ‌Korean ​tradition, ‌closely ​related ‌names ​in ‌the ‌corpus ​include [[baekdusan|Baekdusan]], ​[[chilsong|Chilsong]], ​[[dangun|Dangun]], ​[[halmoni|Halmoni]], ‌[[hananim|Hwanin]], ‌and ​[[jowangshin|Jowangshin]].

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, or ‌artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex corpus ​is ‌yet ​assigned ​to ‌Hwanung with ​certainty. ‌That ​absence ‌should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ​Korean ‌name of ​this ‌type ​the ‌material ​record is ‌expected ​to ‌be ​thin, ​and the ‌primary ‌evidence ‌remains ​the ​textual testimony ‌gathered ​in ​the ‌Scholarly ​Sources section[^1].

​Were ‌such ​evidence ‌to surface, ​it ​would ​take ​recognizable ‌forms: votive ‌or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ​naming ​환웅 (桓雄), ‌sanctuary ‌or ‌cult ‌remains ​tied to ‌son ​of ​heaven ​and ‌iconography matching ​its ​traditional ​attributes ‌(sandalwood ​tree and ​three ​heavenly ‌seals). ​Each ‌candidate would ​be ‌weighed ​against ‌the ‌reconstructed form ​of ​the ​name ​before ‌entering the ‌scholarly ​record.
